title: Field-Induced Dissociation Reveals Excitonic Long-Range Photocarrier Transport in Bulk-Insulating Bi2Se3 Nanoribbons
authors: Rodrigo Becerra Silva, Xiang Yi, Ziyi Song, Dong Yu
abstract: Photoexcited charge carriers in topological insulators display anomalously long-range transport at cryogenic temperatures, but the underlying mechanism remains under debate. Here we use a transverse electric field as a discriminating probe of photocarrier dynamics in bulk-insulating Sb-doped Bi2Se3 nanoribbons, combining scanning photocurrent microscopy (SPCM) with ultrafast transient photovoltage (TPV) measurements. SPCM shows that suppression of the photocurrent requires a transverse electric field nearly 50 times larger than that needed to deflect free carriers, yet comparable to the expected exciton dissociation field. TPV measurements at 12 K and low excitation fluence reveal that the photocarrier diffusivity exceeds the value implied by the Einstein relation and the measured drift mobility by more than an order of magnitude, a bound that holds even at the lower end of the fitting uncertainty. Together, these observations indicate that the long-range photoresponse is not carried by free charge carriers but by a charge-neutral correlated state.
summary: The paper investigates the mechanism behind long-range photocarrier transport in topological insulator nanoribbons by comparing measurements under an external electric field against free-carrier theory. By observing that the required field to suppress photocurrent far exceeds theoretical limits for free charges, and by showing diffusivity violations in time-domain measurements, the authors conclude that excitons—a charge-neutral correlated state—are responsible for the observed transport.
main_problem: The study aims to determine the physical mechanism responsible for anomalously long-range photocarrier transport observed in topological insulators at cryogenic temperatures.
main_result: The evidence strongly indicates that this long-range photoresponse is not carried by free charge carriers but rather by a charge-neutral correlated state, such as an exciton condensate.
method: The researchers combined Scanning Photocurrent Microscopy (SPCM) and ultrafast Transient Photovoltage (TPV) measurements, using the application of a transverse electric field as a discriminating probe.
model_or_system: The physical system is bulk-insulating Sb-doped Bi2Se3 nanoribbons. The analysis compares experimental results against theoretical models for both free charge carrier diffusion/drift and exciton dissociation dynamics (Poole-Frenkel type).
key_observables: Photocurrent suppression threshold field ($E_{th}$), photocarrier diffusivity, and the ratio $(D/\mu)/(k_B T/q)$ derived from TPV measurements.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures (e.g., 12 K), transverse electric fields ($\sim 33 	ext{ mV}/\mu	ext{m}$ vs $\sim 0.7 	ext{ mV}/\mu	ext{m}$ benchmark), and excitation fluence.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the transverse field acts as a discriminator between charged (deflected) and neutral (undeformed) carriers, and that the exciton dissociation follows a Poole-Frenkel type relationship.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate SPCM maps showing field dependence of photocurrent suppression, comparisons to free carrier simulations, and TPV analysis plots detailing photovoltage decay and diffusivity ratios.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the anomalous transport using SPCM (field dependence), then providing independent confirmation via TPV measurements (diffusivity violation), and finally synthesizing these results across temperature and fluence dependencies to rule out free carriers in favor of excitons.
why_interesting: This work provides a clear experimental distinction between single-particle transport and collective, correlated excitations (excitons) using field-dependent optical probes, which is highly relevant for understanding strongly interacting quantum matter systems.
